svg.title: Kadane's Algorithm and Cyclic Sort: Dynamic Reset vs In-Place Permutation
svg.desc: Animated visualization of Kadane's algorithm evaluating currentSum = max(nums[i], currentSum + nums[i]) to find maximum subarray sum 6 on [-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5], paired with Cyclic Sort placing integers [1..n] into correctIdx = nums[i] - 1 in O(n) time and O(1) space.
svg.text: Kadane's Algorithm & Cyclic Sort: Linear DP Reset vs In-Place Permutation
Local Extend-vs-Reset Subarray Recurrence max(nums[i], currentSum + nums[i]) & O(n) Home-Index Swapping

g.text: Start with single-element subarray [-2] (handles all-negative inputs).
Negative prefix (-2) hurts! Discard prefix and start fresh at 1.
Extending beats starting at -3, but currentSum is now negative (-2).
Discard negative prefix (-2); start new optimal subarray at index 3 (4).
Running sum +3 remains positive, so keeping prefix [4, -1] helps future items!
Prefix [4, -1] boosted 2 up to 5. New maxSum = 5!
currentSum drops to 1, while maxSum preserves best seen (6).

svg.text: Invariant: currentSum = max sum of any subarray ending strictly at index i.
Why Kadane Works Where Sliding Window Fails
Sliding Window requires non-negative elements. Kadane handles arbitrary
negatives because it only needs to track ONE bit of history:
currentSum < 0 => prefix is strictly harmful -> reset to nums[i]
Initialize both currentSum = nums[0] and maxSum = nums[0] (never 0!).

g.text: Places 3 permanently at index 2. Do NOT increment i yet!
Places 2 permanently at index 1. 3 is already locked at index 2.
Places 5 permanently at index 4. Three elements now settled!
Places 4 at index 3 and brings 1 into index 0 simultaneously!
Element is in its home slot (or duplicate at home slot) -> advance i.
i=1..4: all nums[i] === i + 1 -> sorted in O(n)!
Total iterations = 4 swaps + 5 advances = 9 <= 2n (at most n-1 swaps).

svg.text: Why no infinite loop? Each swap locks at least 1 element at its final index.
Checking `nums[i] !== nums[correctIdx]` prevents infinite self-swaps on
duplicates and naturally reveals missing/duplicate numbers in O(1) space!
Both algorithms run in strictly O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space without allocating DP tables or sorting in O(n log n).
